title: Booking API Design
description: Design a booking API for reservations, availability, and cancellations with conflict prevention and idempotent holds.

data.text: Booking APIs must prevent double-booking while remaining responsive under high concurrency. A flight, hotel room, or event seat can only be sold once. You need atomic holds, timeouts, and a clear state machine for reservations.

data.title: Resources
items: Venues — hotels, theaters, or event locations
Resources — rooms, seats, or tables within a venue
Availability — date/time slots when a resource is bookable
Bookings — reservations with status and expiry

data.text: A booking transitions through states to prevent abuse and allow cleanup of abandoned reservations.

items: EXPIRED — hold timed out without payment

data.title: POST /holds — Reserve a resource without payment
data.content: A hold is an atomic reservation with a TTL. If the client does not confirm within the TTL, the hold expires and the resource becomes available again.

data.text: Two clients must never receive confirmation for the same resource. Use atomic operations in your data store. Redis Lua scripts or SQL advisory locks are common patterns.

data.title: POST /holds/{id}/confirm
data.content: Confirming a hold requires a payment token. The server validates the hold is still valid, processes payment, and converts the hold to a confirmed booking.

data.title: Hold expiry enforcement
data.text: Use a background job or Redis key expiry event to release expired holds automatically. Do not rely on clients to cancel. If a hold expires, return 404 on subsequent confirm attempts.

items.question: Can a user hold multiple seats at once?
items.answer: Yes, but enforce a per-user hold limit (e.g., max 6 seats) to prevent scalping. Use a transaction to validate and hold all seats atomically.

items.question: What happens if payment succeeds but the hold expired?
items.answer: Payment should be processed inside the same atomic transaction as hold confirmation. If the hold is invalid, refund immediately and return 409 Conflict.

items.question: Should I expose internal resource IDs to clients?
items.answer: Use opaque, non-guessable IDs for holds and bookings. Sequential IDs enable scraping and scalping. UUIDs or ULIDs are preferred.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Booking is a state machine: HELD -> CONFIRMED -> CANCELLED/EXPIRED.
Atomic holds prevent double-booking under concurrent requests.
Background expiry cleanup keeps inventory accurate without client cooperation.
Idempotency keys make payment retries safe.
data.takeaway: The core problem in booking APIs is concurrency. Solve it with atomic holds, enforce expiry server-side, and make payment a single atomic transition.
